prompt: Match each lambda to its function type.
hint: Parameters in parentheses, an arrow, the result.

prompt: `addBreak` is a `(Int) -> Int`. What is `addBreak(45)` on the JVM?
hint: Printing `addBreak` showed what it is underneath.

choices.text: A jump to a function pointer
choices.why: The JVM has no function pointers; a lambda is an object.
Right: every lambda is an object with an `invoke` method.

choices.text: A call to a static method named `addBreak` that the compiler generated
choices.why: `addBreak` is a local `val`, not a method; the call goes through the object.

choices.text: A string lookup by the name `addBreak`
choices.why: Nothing is looked up by name at run time.

prompt: Which type is "an optional callback that takes an `Int`"?
hint: Where the `?` sits decides what is optional.

choices.why: That is a function that is always there and returns a `Unit?`.
That is a function whose parameter is optional, not the function itself.
Right: the parentheses put the `?` on the whole function type.
That is not Kotlin syntax.

prompt: When can a lambda use `it`?
hint: `val half: (Int) -> Int = { it / 2 }`.

choices.why: With two parameters there is no `it`; both need names.

choices.text: With one parameter of a known type
choices.why: Right: `it` is the implicit name of that one parameter.
`it` belongs to lambdas, not to loops.

choices.text: Only when the lambda is a single line long
choices.why: A multi-line lambda can use `it` too, though naming it reads better there.

prompt: What does a multi-line lambda give back?
hint: `describe` ended with a string template.

choices.why: A bare `return` is refused in a lambda.
The result is the last expression, declared type or not.

choices.text: The value of its last expression
choices.why: Right: `"$hours h $rest min"` was the result.

choices.text: The value of its first expression
choices.why: The earlier lines are steps; the last one is the answer.

prompt: `val double: (Int) -> Int = { m -> return m * 2 }` inside `main`. Why is the `return` refused?
hint: A bare `return` belongs to something.

choices.text: It would return from `main`, the nearest `fun`
choices.why: Right: the lambda is not a `fun`, so the `return` is not its own.
The `val` is beside the point; it is the lambda that matters.
Parentheses change nothing here.
`{ m -> m * 2 }` returns a number perfectly well.

prompt: `week = listOf(45, 30, 60, 90, 20)`. What is `countWhere(week, { it >= 60 })`?
hint: 60 counts.

prompt: What does `scaledBy(2)(45)` return, where `scaledBy(factor)` returns `{ it * factor }`?
hint: The first call builds a function; the second calls it.

prompt: What does passing the test as a parameter buy `countWhere`?
hint: Five questions about sessions.

choices.text: It runs faster than a loop
choices.why: It is a loop; speed is not the gain.

choices.text: The compiler checks the test at run time
choices.why: The compiler checks the lambda's type at compile time, as always.

choices.text: It lets `countWhere` change the list while counting
choices.why: It reads the list; nothing changes it.

choices.text: One loop, and a line per question
choices.why: Right: the varying part is the argument.

prompt: What is `repeat(2) { … }`?
hint: Look for it in the standard library.

choices.why: It only looks like one.

choices.text: A library function and a trailing lambda
choices.why: Right: `repeat(times: Int, action: (Int) -> Unit)`.
Kotlin has no macros; it is inline, which is different.
Those arrive in lesson 14.

prompt: Which parameter's lambda can be written after the parentheses?

choices.text: Any parameter of a function type
choices.why: Only one can trail, and it is not any one.
The first stayed inside the parentheses in `check`.

choices.text: The last parameter, when it is a function
choices.why: Right: only the last one trails.
The name is irrelevant; the position decides.

prompt: With the standard library, the number of long sessions is `week.___ { it >= 60 }`.
hint: The function `countWhere` turns out to be.

prompt: What is the type of `String::length`?
hint: The object becomes the first parameter.

choices.why: That would be a bound reference to one string.
Right: it takes the string and gives its length.
The arrow points the other way.
A reference is a function, not the result of calling it.

prompt: `val kotlin = "Kotlin"` and `val f = kotlin::startsWith`. What is `f("Kot")`?
hint: A bound reference already has its object.

choices.text: A compile error: `startsWith` needs two arguments
choices.why: The object is already bound, so only the prefix is left.
Right: `"Kotlin".startsWith("Kot")`.
`startsWith` checks a prefix, which `Kot` is.
`startsWith` answers yes or no.

prompt: Which of these cannot be written as a function reference?
hint: A reference only forwards.

choices.why: That is `::isLong`.
That is `String::length`.
Right: the negation is something a reference cannot add.
That is `::format`.

prompt: `var total = 0`, `val add: (Int) -> Unit = { total += it }`, then `add(45)` and `add(30)`. What does `total` hold?
hint: The lambda holds the variable, not a copy.

choices.text: 0, because the lambda changed its own copy
choices.why: There is no copy; Kotlin captures the variable.

choices.text: It does not compile: lambdas may only read local variables
choices.why: That is Java's rule; Kotlin allows the change.
Right: both calls changed `main`'s `total`.
`+=` adds; it does not replace.

prompt: `val next = makeCounter()`, then `next()`, `next()`, `val other = makeCounter()`, `other()`, `next()`. What does the last call return?
hint: Each counter holds its own `count`.

prompt: `var course = "Kotlin"`, `val show = { println(course) }`, `course = "Android"`, `show()`. What prints, and why?
hint: When does the lambda read the variable?

choices.text: `Kotlin`, the value when the lambda was written
choices.why: That needs a `val` copy taken before the lambda.

choices.text: `Android`: it reads the variable when run
choices.why: Right: it holds the variable, not its old value.

choices.text: A compile error about reassigning a captured `var`
choices.why: Kotlin allows it.

choices.text: Nothing; the lambda was discarded when `course` changed
choices.why: Changing a variable does not discard the lambda that holds it.

prompt: What does `inline` on a function that takes a lambda do?
hint: Lesson 1's `println` was one.

choices.text: Copies its body and the lambda's into each call site
choices.why: Right: no lambda object and no call through it at run time.

choices.text: Runs the lambda on another thread
choices.why: Inlining has nothing to do with threads.

choices.text: Caches the lambda's result after its first call
choices.why: Nothing is cached; the code is copied.

choices.text: Forbids the lambda from capturing variables
choices.why: An inlined lambda reads variables as before.

prompt: `printUntilLong(listOf(45, 90, 30))` uses `return@forEach` when an item is 60 or more. What does it print?
hint: A labelled return leaves the lambda only.

choices.why: That would be a bare `return`, leaving the whole function.
90 hits the `return@forEach` before printing.
Right: it skips 90, like `continue`, and finishes.
`return@forEach` does not stop the iteration, only that item.

prompt: Which of these compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: A bare `return` is allowed in a lambda only when it is inlined into a `fun`.

choices.text: `fun f(w: List<Int>): Int? { w.forEach { if (it > 0) return it }; return null }`
choices.why: Yes: `forEach` is inline, so the `return` leaves `f`.

choices.text: `fun g() { twice { return } }`, with `twice` not inline
choices.why: No: that is `NotInline.kt`'s refusal.
Yes: one parameter of a known type, so `it` works.
No: nothing says what `it` is, so its type cannot be inferred.

prompt: Rewrite `countWhere(week, { m -> isLong(m) })` step by step. Put the forms in the order the lesson shortened them.
hint: Name, then position, then the library.
